text:
RAM is not totally pointless for serving massively parallel requests while keeping the energy bill low

IIRC PLE traffic is something like a few hundred kb per second per request, but the issue is that you want to keep the GPU fed quickly to maximise energy usage as idling takes energy too, so that's why all the big inference providers put PLE into RAM or at least keep a hot cache of engrams in RAM. Something like 1% of engram table is responsible for 80-90% of the traffic IIRC so the cache can be surprisingly small (but bigger than you'd expect because the 1% depends on the domain and you can be getting very varied requests if you're a generic inference provider)

SO that's why all the RAM offload code exists. But it's true that SSD offload is good enough for a lot of the use cases here (which is like, mostly agentic coding...)
label: analysis

text:
Ha, finally some engineering talk. The original design was for en-grams to be fully stored in RAM, in practice it turns out as you say the call distribution is wildly lopsided unlike with experts in MoE models, so storing a fraction in RAM is more practical for scaled down use. In my own testing for example I found you can trivially store the image encoder in RAM, for the occasional image in a prompt you lose barely a few ms in encode, in return you free up VRAM without turning your model blind.

The fruit is quite low hanging for optimisations here.
